This functional is designed to enhance the precision of DMRG calculations for larger systems. The transcorrelated method addresses limitations in DMRG by incorporating non-dynamic correlation effects through a coordinate transformation that optimizes the wave function. This study introduces a perturbation scheme designed to address stochastic uncertainty in the initial locations of particles within the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) framework. By utilizing a specific method to propagate this location uncertainty over time, the approach ensures the conservation of mass and guarantees that the perturbation vanishes asymptotically as time progresses further.

Randomization is fundamental to both data storage and processing within the realm of big data. This paper introduces a fresh approach to random number generation grounded in the principles of homomorphic encryption. We present the first implementation of a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) utilizing fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). This system leverages FHE's capabilities to execute bitwise operations, specifically XOR and AND, which are essential components of the widely used linear feedback shift register (LFSR) architecture. We detail the methodology for implementing these registers within FHE and evaluate the algorithm's performance against standard software-based PRNGs. Our findings indicate that our FHE-based generator achieves a security level comparable to conventional PRNGs while surpassing them in efficiency.

This paper presents SafeAPT, an algorithm designed to adapt robotic policies from simulation to the real world while ensuring safety. The approach integrates two key components: a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that learns a dynamics model and employs model predictive control (MPC) to generate safe actions, complemented by a safety-adaptive reward function. This study examines the relationship between radio structures and jets in radio galaxies, utilizing a sample of 100 objects from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) that exhibit strong radio emission and are classified via the Fanaroff-Riley (FR) scheme. The analysis employs the Galaxy Zoo2 (GZ2) classification system, which categorizes galaxies into 12 distinct morphological classes. The results indicate that the majority of these FR sources display radio structures, with 68% classified as FR I and 32% as FR II. The findings demonstrate a strong correlation between the FR classification and the specific radio morphology, particularly regarding the presence of hotspots and jets. Specifically, the absence of jets and hotspots is prevalent in FR I galaxies, whereas FR II galaxies typically exhibit these features. Additionally, the study reveals a significant link between the FR classification and the host galaxy's environment, noting that FR II galaxies are more frequently found in galaxy clusters compared to their FR I counterparts.

This study introduces a nonparametric approach to test the equivalence of regression functions, applicable to both continuous and discontinuous scenarios without imposing structural constraints. The methodology relies on a new test statistic derived from the $L_2$-distance between functions, which is assessed against simulated null distributions. The paper demonstrates that the test maintains the correct significance level and achieves strong power across a diverse range of simulated functions. Additionally, the methodology is applied to analyze data from a clinical trial evaluating the efficacy of the drug Abilify in treating schizophrenia.

This study investigates the efficacy of multilingual models versus monolingual models for analyzing social media content. We examine a suite of multilingual architectures, including mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, and mBERT, and benchmark them against language-specific models trained on XLMR. To address the scarcity of high-quality, multilingual datasets, we introduce a new collection of multilingual Twitter data comprising 1.2 million tweets across 10 languages. This dataset is utilized to train and evaluate our proposed models. Our findings indicate that while multilingual models generally outperform their unilingual counterparts, specific scenarios exist where unilingual models yield superior results. Additionally, we analyze the impact of varying training data volumes on model performance.

Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) is a widely utilized imaging technique for assessing brain activity. While deep learning has recently been applied to various medical fields, its use in brain disorder classification via fMRI remains limited. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to classify brain diseases using fMRI data. The proposed architecture integrates a 3D convolutional neural network with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to process volumetric data. The 3D CNN extracts spatial features from the images, whereas the LSTM component identifies temporal patterns across these volumes. This end-to-end model was evaluated on a dataset comprising 1,000 fMRI scans from 250 subjects with schizophrenia and 250 healthy controls. The results demonstrate that the method achieves a classification accuracy of 85.5%, surpassing the performance of traditional machine learning approaches.

This article examines the stability of linear systems under nonlinear feedback, with a specific focus on convergence rate analysis. The study introduces a straightforward methodology for estimating the speed of convergence applicable to both continuous and discontinuous nonlinear functions. By linking this approach to an analysis of dissipation energies, the proposed method offers an intuitive and effective framework. The utility of these estimators is demonstrated through two practical applications: first, in the field of control theory regarding the regulation of a pendulum, and second, in the modeling of the plastic deformation of metals.

The approach further incorporates a specialized boundary treatment that ensures the stability and accuracy of the high-order viscary scheme by enforcing a consistent weak formulation of the Navier-Stokes equations at the domain boundaries. This study investigates how a photonic crystal (PhC) back reflector influences the optical absorption in ultrathin silicon films. We analyze the absorption spectra of silicon layers ranging from 100 nm to 200 nm thickness, which are paired with a photonic crystal back reflector. Our results demonstrate that this PhC back reflector significantly enhances absorption across the investigated silicon thickness range. Furthermore, we examine the impact of PhC design parameters on absorption characteristics, revealing a strong correlation between absorption and the PhC's periodicity.

Valuation algebra is a mathematical framework designed to facilitate the management and manipulation of uncertain information. This paper extends that algebra to include credal sets, which represent collections of probability distributions. We define fundamental operations for these sets—including addition, multiplication, and minimization—and demonstrate that credal sets can be treated as valuations within the algebraic structure of complete lattices. Leveraging lattice theory, we introduce two distinct forms of association. The first form, utilizing standard lattice operations, generalizes traditional probabilistic combination methods. The second form, grounded in lattice residuation, extends arithmetic multiplication specifically for stochastic networks.

Distance-based recommendation systems are a prominent category of algorithms that rank items according to their proximity to a user, typically by calculating distances between the user and the items. However, these traditional methods often rely on simplistic distance metrics that fail to account for the internal structures of items, thereby limiting their effectiveness. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel model that leverages the Wasserstein distance to estimate user-item proximity. The approach involves representing both the user and items as probability distributions and computing the distance between them using the Wasserstein metric. To capture the item's internal structure, we utilize a neural network to generate a distribution over its attributes, while for the user, we derive a distribution based on the item attributes the user has historically interacted with. Our experimental results demonstrate that this model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of recommendation quality.

This study examines the influence of a non-Markovian environment on the dynamics of an open quantum system, specifically a qubit, utilizing the quasi-exactly non-Markovian (ENM) generalized amplitude damping (GAD) channel. We demonstrate that the quasi-ENM GAD channel exhibits non-Markovian characteristics that differ substantially from the traditional eternally non-markovian property. Furthermore, we establish that the non-Markovian behavior of this channel is contingent upon the initial state of the qubit, a finding that diverges from the standard definition of eternally non-markovian channels. Additionally, we analyze the relationship between the non-Markovian traits of the quasi-ENM GAD channel and the non-equilibrium dynamics of the qubit, revealing that non-equilibrium effects are amplified when the channel operates in a non-Markovian regime.

This paper introduces CCRAL (Coarse-to-Fine Contrastive Representation Alignment), a new technique designed to enhance model generalization for testing datasets not encountered during training. The method operates on the premise that representations for similar samples should cluster together, while dissimilar ones should remain separated. By leveraging a coarse-to-fine contrastive learning framework, CRRAL aligns the feature space of unseen data with that of training data, effectively mitigating the gap between training and testing distributions. The approach consists of two stages: first, a coarse alignment phase uses a pre-trained model to roughly map features of unseen data into the training space, followed by a second phase that employs a fine-tuning strategy to adjust these features for closer alignment with ideal targets. The final stage utilizes a contrastive loss function to optimize the representation of unseen inputs, ensuring they closely match prototypes derived from training data. Theoretical analysis confirms that CRRAL reduces the error between prototype and feature representations, while extensive experiments across multiple image classification benchmarks demonstrate that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

Creating semantic maps is crucial for robotics, yet it presents significant challenges due to the complexity of its tasks. This paper introduces a new approach to semantic mapping that leverages the inherent semantic information found within object categories. By utilizing object detectors, we can extract features such as material, color, and object type, which are then integrated into a standard 2D grid map. This methodology facilitates the automatic generation of maps enriched with semantic details. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric designed to assess the quality of these semantically enhanced maps.

This paper introduces Rikudo, a logic-based puzzle from *Nikke Sourens* that involves connecting numbered nodes with paths. We demonstrate that determining solvability is NP-complete when numbers are distributed randomly; however, the puzzle becomes solvable in polynomial time if all numbers are odd.

Optimization is a fundamental component of machine learning, and the Sinkhorn's algorithm is widely used to solve entropic-regularized optimal transport challenges. This paper introduces a novel variant of the algorithm that accelerates convergence by integrating a preconditioner derived from the Hessian of the Lagrangian. We demonstrate that this pre-conditioned approach attains linear convergence, and we validate its superior performance through experiments involving both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We present the findings of a survey targeting gravitational lens systems that exhibit strong magnification and significant flux magnification ratios. This study focuses on two specific systems, J0818-2613 and J1817+2729, which are ideal for investigating the Hubble tension. By analyzing the flux magnification ratios within these systems, we can constrain the Hubble constant ($H_0$) and the Hubble tension parameter ($\Delta H_0$). These results align with the redshifts derived from spectroscopic observations. Furthermore, we determine the flux magnification ratios to be $1.11\pm0.11$ and $1.11\pm0.11$ for the respective systems. These values are consistent with the theoretical expectations for the Hubble tension. Our findings provide a new constraint on the Hubble tension, which is consistent with the standard model. This study addresses a generalized form of the $q$-difference equation. The primary objective is to determine solutions for this class of equations, which are defined by a $q$-difference operator acting on a $q$-difference fractional derivative. The $q$-difference fractional derivative utilized here is the Riemann-Liouville type. The analysis covers both initial and boundary value problems. The methodology involves applying the $q$-difference analogue of the Laplace transform to resolve initial value problems and utilizing Green's functions to address boundary value problems. The paper also provides illustrative examples for each case.

This study investigates the phonon Hall effect (PHE) in dielectric materials, revealing that a magnetic field can generate a transverse heat flux driven by the Lorentz force acting on phonons. While previous research established that the linear dielectric response can induce a PHE, our findings demonstrate that the linear phonon drag effect yields a significantly larger PHE magnitude. Specifically, we show that the linear dielectric response is often negligible compared to the drag contribution. Additionally, we analyze how the drag-induced PHE varies with temperature and the strength of the magnetic field.

Wide-field imaging setups, such as those utilizing a large number of lenses, are prone to optical aberrations that degrade image quality. To address this, we introduce a nod-and-shuffle method designed to enhance image fidelity. This approach involves capturing a series of images with the detector sequentially moved across the field of view, thereby distributing optical aberrations across the detector and compressing the field into a smaller area. This compression facilitates the identification of field-of-view (FOV) losses, which can then be corrected through image stitching. Our analysis demonstrates that this technique significantly reduces acquisition times, achieving a 2.5-fold improvement over traditional techniques. We also present a new image reconstruction algorithm that leverages the nod-and-shuffle data to generate a high-fidelity, stitched image. This algorithm utilizes a deep learning-based denoising network to compress the data, followed by a stitching process that employs a deep learning-based registration network to align image pairs. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and experimental results using a nod-and-shuffle lenslet array.

This paper establishes novel inequalities that serve as replacements for the matrix analogues of the Chebyschek sum inequality and related variants. Furthermore, it demonstrates additional inequalities equivalent to these main results.

The Internet of Things (IoT) has become a significant area of research, attracting substantial interest from both industry and academia. Currently, ICS testbeds are the primary resources used to study the security aspects of Industrial Control Systems. However, the varying maturity levels of these facilities often result in inconsistent and difficult-to-compare findings. To address this challenge, we introduce a framework for evaluating ICS testbed maturity, grounded in a comprehensive survey of existing testbeds and their associated security research. We propose a maturity assessment model that employs a novel, quantitative maturity index to evaluate testbeds based on specific criteria. Furthermore, we apply Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) to enhance the evaluation of testbeds by identifying areas for improvement. Finally, the study proposes a set of recommendations for upgrading ICS testbeds, illustrated through the case of the testbed at the Institute for the Advancement of Cyber-Physical Systems (IACS).

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has garnered significant attention in recent years, with numerous algorithms developed to address diverse challenges. However, a persistent issue in these algorithms is the tendency for agents to adopt identical policies, resulting in a lack of diversity in their behaviors. This paper introduces a new method for enhancing policy diversity in MARL by leveraging greedy-based value representation (GVR). GVR estimates the value of a policy by combining the maximum and minimum Q-values for each action, thereby guiding agents to select policies that maximize this greedy value. By explicitly promoting diversity in policy selection, GVR effectively mitigates the problem of homogeneous behavior. We integrated GVR into the QMIX algorithm, yielding a new variant called QMIX-GVR. Empirical evaluations on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) benchmark demonstrate that QMIX-GVR surpasses the original QMIX algorithm in both the "easy" and "medium" difficulty settings.

We introduce StereoSet, a resource designed to assess stereotypical biases across four domains: gender, race, age, and occupation. Unlike prior works limited to a single domain, our approach extends bias measurement to these additional areas. To ensure high-quality data, we employed crowdsourcing to collect word pairs representing each domain, followed by extensive human validation and the application of multiple automated metrics to refine stereoptical associations. To demonstrate the utility of this resource, we present a new metric for measuring bias in embeddings and evaluate various word2vec models using our dataset. Additionally, we show that the proposed metric effectively captures bias reductions resulting from debiasing techniques. Finally, we introduce a straightforward, linear post-processing method that significantly lowers gender bias across multiple algorithms without compromising model performance.

This study introduces a Contextual Multi-Armed Bandit (CMAB) framework designed to learn the optimal policy for adjusting link tilts in network optimization. The CMAB approach models the tilt adjustment process as a sequence of sequential decisions, where the tilt of a link is updated based on the current traffic demand and the previously modified links. We demonstrate that a link's improvement in a given time step is influenced by the traffic profile and the set of links already altered. Additionally, we establish theoretical bounds regarding the CMAB algorithm's regret and convergence speed. To validate these findings, we conducted extensive simulations using a real-world traffic dataset, which confirmed the theoretical convergence guarantees and highlighted the algorithm's efficiency.

This analysis determines CKM angle gamma using semileptonic decays of B mesons, specifically B^0 \to \rho \pi and B^0 \to K^* K. The study utilizes 3.0 fb^{-1} of data collected by the LHCb experiment from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. The gamma angle is derived from an interference term involving B^0 \to \rho \pi decays and CP-conjugate processes, alongside interference between B^0 \to K^* K decays and their CP-conjugate counterparts. The measured value for gamma is 66.0^{+10.0}_{-7.0} (stat) ^{+10.0}_{-6.0} (sys) degrees, with a 95.5% confidence level.

This work aims to extend the application of complex symmetry in convex geometry. We demonstrate that convex bodies can alternatively be characterized through the equivalence of their orthogonal projections and complex symmetries. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the volume of a convex body's orthogonal projection and the integral of volumes of its associated transversal sections, calculated over the unit sphere.

The rise of the digital economy has prompted extensive research into the economic dimensions of data, specifically examining how data serves as a commodity, functions within markets, and drives trade. However, current frameworks largely rely on established economic theories, often neglecting the perspectives of individuals regarding their personal data. This study bridges that gap by analyzing how laypeople value transactions involving their personal data, with a specific focus on the role of reciprocity. We conducted a qualitative study featuring 20 in-depth interviews with participants recruited from a broad demographic. Our findings reveal that these consumers frequently view data transactions as reciprocal exchanges, a dynamic that frequently clashes with existing economic models. Furthermore, our analysis identifies three primary drivers of this reciprocity: the nature of the data involved, the characteristics of the transaction, and the anticipated benefits. Finally, we discuss how these insights can inform the design of a more equitable data ecosystem.

This study introduces a deep learning approach designed to detect and correct symbol timing errors in FTN signaling. The proposed method utilizes a deep neural network (DNN) to estimate the timing offset, followed by a secondary DNN to convert this offset into a corrected, discrete symbol time. The paper presents simulation results that demonstrate the efficacy of the suggested technique, showing that it significantly lowers detection complexity compared to exhaustive search methods while achieving performance equivalent to the optimal Maximum Likelihood (ML) approach.

This work examines continuity effects within the effect algebra of a complete distributive lattice $L$ by analyzing two specific structures: the Frink ideal topology and the order topology. We establish that, provided $L$ is atomic, these topologies are equivalent. The findings extend known results regarding continuity in lattice effect algebras back to the broader context of general distributive lattices.

This study introduces SaliencyMix, a novel data augmentation technique designed to enhance model robustness in object detection. The approach leverages attention maps from the source model to identify salient regions, using these features to guide the fusion of images from different sources. We demonstrate that SaliencyMix outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, including CutMix and Mixup, across various object detection benchmarks. Additionally, our analysis reveals that CutMix and Mixup are susceptible to adversarial attacks, whereas SaliencyMix exhibits significantly stronger resistance.

We introduce a novel method for investigating modified gravity that leverages intrinsic alignments within the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) signal. This approach utilizes the cross-correlation of a galaxy distribution with an intrinsic alignment field to measure a BAO-mode-dependent signal that is sensitive to modifications in gravity. By employing a simplified toy model, we demonstrate that this technique can constrain the gravitational alignment parameter, $M_A$, with a precision of approximately 10%. Furthermore, we outline a strategy to mitigate the impact of redshift-space distortions on the alignment signal, which are typically caused by redshift-space distortions.

Soft-deformable particle systems, including networks of entangled polymers, exhibit memory effects by retaining a distinct internal state linked to their deformation history. This study utilizes a simplified model of a single loop tethered to a sphere to investigate how individual components contribute to this phenomenon. By analyzing the system's response to specific cyclic strain protocols, we identify a "memory variable"—defined as the accumulated strain history—that effectively predicts the particle distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this internal state can be reversibly cycled between two distinct values through controlled strain reversal. These findings offer a clear, intuitive framework for grasping the origins of memory effects in soft materials and suggest new avenues for designing materials capable of memorizing deformation.

We present a computational investigation into the thermodynamic stability of gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) and their phase transitions, utilizing a machine learning (ML) potential trained on density functional theory (DFT) data. This ML framework incorporates a specialized finite-size correction to accurately model surface effects, enabling precise calculation of absolute free energies for both face-centered cubic (fcc) and icosahedral structures. Our findings indicate that fcc configurations remain thermodynamically stable across all particle sizes, whereas icosahedral forms are only stable in smaller nanoparticles. We observe a size-dependent decline in the melting temperature of AuNPs, which aligns with prior experimental and theoretical results. Furthermore, the study identifies a critical size threshold at approximately 3.5 nm, below which the melting temperature drops precipitously.

This brief communication demonstrates that relaxing conventional assumptions on differentiability can effectively extend the scope of research concerning quasi-linear elliptic boundary value problems.

This study introduces a model based on the gauge symmetry $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y \times U(1)_X$, where $U(X)$ is an abelian extension. Within this framework, a new $U(X)$ gauge boson, denoted as $X$, is generated. The model's particle content is designed to address the $U(1)_X$ anomaly through a specific mechanism. Additionally, a horizontal correlation exists between quarks and anti-leptons, a feature that allows the model to resolve several experimental anomalies associated with non-standard interactions.

This study establishes identities involving $(h; q)$-Genocchi polynomials and numbers by utilizing generating functions and the operational method. Additionally, it derives identities for $(h; q)$-Genocchi and Bernoulli numbers and polynomials through the application of both the operational procedure and Cauchy's formula. Finally, it examines the relationships between $(h; q)$-Genocchi objects and $zeta$-functions at negative integers, as well as the connection to $p$-adic $zeta$-functions evaluated at negative integers.

This study introduces a reinforcement learning framework for tackling nonstationary problems by estimating average rewards. The proposed algorithm leverages a novel incremental gradient method to adaptively learn optimal policies, with convergence proven under the assumption of bounded nonstationarity. Additionally, the work addresses the challenge of estimating bounded regret in online settings. Empirical results from a simulated linear system demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard for assessing treatment efficacy, yet their conclusions are often limited by confounding factors arising from non-random participant attrition. To address this, the study introduces a novel estimator for the causal odds ratio (COR), a metric that is more interpretable than average treatment effects and better suited for binary outcomes. This new estimator, which is consistent and asymptotically normally distributed, relies on a semiparametric framework that requires no assumptions about the underlying data distribution. We also present a closed-form solution for the COR, which is more efficient than the standard logit regression estimator. Empirical results from both simulated datasets and real-world data indicate that our method offers superior performance compared to existing alternatives.

Autoencoders serve as a versatile tool for learning latent representations, yet their utility is often limited by the inability to guarantee a bijective mapping between input and latent spaces. This paper introduces a method for constructing invertible autoencoders by decomposing the mapping into a sequence of invertible layers, each transforming the data distribution into a known form. We demonstrate that the total loss for this architecture is a sum of individual losses, enabling straightforward optimization. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical framework linking the model's capacity to the count of invertible layers. Our findings indicate that incorporating invertible layers enhances both log-likelihood and sample quality, particularly in high-dimensional settings. Additionally, we show that these layers can be integrated into standard autoencoder designs to bolster performance.

Smart cities are increasingly generating vast quantities of data, necessitating the development of visualization platforms to support the identification of patterns and the formulation of data-driven decisions. This paper introduces a system designed to visualize smart city datasets, featuring a user interface for data exploration and a set of algorithms for analytical processing. The system's core is a data structure that organizes information into a multi-dimensional space, allowing users to navigate and explore it freely. Additionally, it incorporates a set of algorithms capable of generating visual representations of specific data aspects, including pattern recognition and anomaly detection. The paper details the system's design and implementation, along with a demonstration of its utility through a case study.

This study introduces optimal multigrid-based geometric multigrid preconditioners tailored for hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin methods (HdG) utilizing piecewise linear elements. These preconditioners are designed to ensure convergence rates that remain constant regardless of the method's polynomial degree. The approach involves constructing a coarse grid system with degree $k-1$ derived from a $k$th-degree fine grid system, followed by applying a specific $k$th-degree HdG preconditioner to the resulting multigrid operator. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical experiments.

The $E$-value serves as a metric for assessing the minimum magnitude of unmeasured confounding required to sustain a causal inference in observational studies. This paper extends that concept to scenarios involving missing data by introducing a corresponding $E$-value framework. This adaptation enables researchers to quantify how much missing data must be assumed to be missing at random before a null hypothesis can invalidate their original causal claim. We demonstrate that this generalized approach retains the same fundamental characteristics as the traditional $E$-value, specifically its capacity to be interpreted in terms of the plausibility of assuming missingness is random under varying levels of weight. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this method through an application to data from a study on COVID-19 vaccination and mortality.

In crossover trials, which typically involve few participants and consequently face a high risk of missing data, this issue poses a significant challenge. While parametric imputation methods are commonly employed to address gaps, they often fail to account for the uncertainty inherent in filling in missing values. This paper introduces a novel Bayesian imputation technique specifically designed for crossover data, utilizing a mixed-effects model to impute missing treatments and baseline values. The approach incorporates a noninformative prior to represent imputation uncertainty, with the model's remaining parameters estimated via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. The efficacy of this method is evaluated through a comparison against a standard parametric approach using a simulation study. The proposed method is further applied to a real-world dataset from a clinical trial investigating the treatment of depression.

This work demonstrates that the nerve of a category naturally supports the structure of a $A_\infty$ relative to a category. Additionally, it is shown that the geometric realization of the $A_n$ nerve of a category converges to its original category in the $A_\infty$ sense as $A_n$ approaches $A_\infty$ in the $A_\infty$ sense.

DRAM Physical Uncloneable Functions (PUFs) are promising candidates for securing Internet of Things (IoT) devices, yet their performance is hindered by low throughput and high sensitivity to environmental variations. This paper introduces a novel DRAM PUF architecture that leverages the inherent stochasticity of DRAM read errors to generate a PUF response. This approach achieves two key advantages: (1) a significantly higher response generation rate compared to current state-of-the-art DRAM PUFs, and (2) enhanced robustness against environmental fluctuations. Experimental results demonstrate that this new PUF design outperforms existing solutions in both speed and stability.

Functional programming has recently gained significant traction in the domains of distributed systems and cloud computing, where its principles of immutability and first-class functions offer a robust framework for managing state and crafting declarative, resilient solutions. This study examines the application of functional programming in orchestrating virtualized network functions within the context of Software-Defined Networking (SDN). By leveraging SDN's centralized, programmable control plane, we propose a novel architecture that utilizes functional programming paradigms to streamline the management of virtual network resources. This approach enables the formulation of resilient, flexible, and scalable workflows for deploying virtual network functions (VNFs) across complex environments. We demonstrate that adopting functional programming yields a resilient architecture, where the immutability of functional data structures safeguards the system against state corruption and ensures operational integrity. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of this proposed architecture, highlighting its efficacy in managing dynamic network conditions and illustrating its potential to enhance the adaptability and efficiency of next-generation SDN-based networks.

The rise of topological quantum computing has spurred the development of benchmarking protocols for quantum gates, with the toric code serving as a leading example. This study introduces a refined version of such a benchmark, designed to evaluate the performance of a specific class of topological gates. We establish that the associated measurement problem can be mapped to the independent variables of the classic "bond-centered" Ising model. This reduction facilitates the application of efficient classical algorithms to estimate gate fidelity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed benchmark can be expressed as a semidefinite program, thereby enabling the derivation of rigorous fidelity lower bounds.

We introduce the Universal Worker System (UWS), a framework designed to manage distributed execution of tasks within large, heterogeneous computing clusters. The system operates by allowing users to submit jobs to a central server, which then distributes tasks to available workers. These workers autonomously select tasks to execute based on their specific capabilities, reporting successful completions back to the server for further instruction. Built on the Message Passing Interface (MPI), UWS supports a wide variety of tasks, including MPI-based applications, MPI scripts, and standard Unix commands.

This article explores the application of blockchain technology in wireless communications and networking, aiming to bolster security and facilitate machine learning. We introduce the concept of "blockchain-enabled learning" (BEL), wherein wireless systems utilize a blockchain to store data and model parameters, thereby enabling decentralized learning. Furthermore, we examine the convergence behavior of a gradient descent algorithm within BEL environments. The analysis demonstrates that under specific conditions, this descent converges to a neighborhood of the optimal solution, with the radius of convergence determined by the block generation rate, the learning rate, and the noise level.

This study investigates the O2/O3 relationship and ozone production in terrestrial exoplanet atmospheres by analyzing a sample of 1000 models. These models vary host star temperature, stellar flux, and planetary atmospheric composition. We find that the O2/O3 relationship is significantly influenced by the host star's temperature. Planets orbiting M-dwarfs exhibit a strong positive correlation between O2 and O3, whereas those around Sun-like stars show a weak or non-existent correlation. This disparity arises because M-dwarf stars have lower temperatures and lower flux, which suppress O3 photolysis and favor O2-driven ozone production. Conversely, Sun-like stars have higher temperatures and flux, leading to O3 photolysis rates that exceed O2-driven production, thereby weakening the O2/O3 correlation. We demonstrate that surface currents are resilient to noise, specifically those in the form of white noise. This robustness is observed in both bosonic and fermionic systems, where the current's ability to withstand the noise is directly linked to the nonlocal characteristics of the topological order. Additionally, we explore the behavior of surface currents within disordered environments and propose a method to characterize these surface phenomena in higher-dimensional topological insulators.

This study presents a multilingual neural machine translation (mNMT) model designed for domain adaptation in medical texts. While current mNMT models excel at cross-lingual translation, they often struggle with domain adaptation, particularly when training data is scarce. We introduce a straightforward yet effective method to adapt a domain out-of-domain (DOD) model to the medical domain (DAA) using a small dataset of parallel medical texts. Our approach involves fine-tuning the DOD model on this data and adding a regularization term to the loss function to encourage the model to retain the linguistic features of the DOD. We evaluated this method by translating medical texts from English into French, German, and Spanish. Results demonstrate that our model outperforms the DOD baseline, achieving higher BLEU scores and lower error rates.

We introduce a novel task, the contrastive context prediction (CCP) task, designed to enhance sentence representation learning within multilingual pre-trained models. Unlike existing methods that rely on a single language model, the CCP task utilizes a shared model to process sentences from multiple languages. This approach requires the model to predict the context of a target language based on its contrastive relationship with contexts from other languages. By enforcing this cross-lingual contrastive learning, the model captures richer, more robust representations. Empirical evaluations on the GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art multilingual models.

This paper introduces a new method for learning multimodal representations by capitalizing on the inherent asynchronous nature of multimodal data. We introduce Prototype-based Modality Rebalance (PMR), a straightforward yet effective technique that leverages prototype distances to establish modality-specific inter-sample relationships. PMR facilitates the learning of discriminative inter-modal structures by encouraging slower modalities to adopt the prototypical patterns of faster ones. Consequently, PMR enhances the robustness of multimodal learning models and significantly outperforms existing baselines. We validated this approach on the challenging benchmark of predicting COVID-19 severity using combined X-ray and CT scans, demonstrating that it yields substantial performance gains.

We examine the derivation of the massless fermion Vlasov equation within the context of the semi-classical limit of the Dirac-Fock-Vlasov system. Our findings indicate that the divergent component of the local particle number density directly influences the kinetic equation, thereby necessitating an adjustment to the standard semi-classical expansion. Furthermore, we establish a rigorous existence theorem for solutions to the Dirac-Fock-Vlasov framework under the assumption of initial data that are nearly stationary.

This study introduces a novel command recognition framework that integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with a Transformer-Dense Neural Network (TT-DNN). The proposed architecture is designed to enhance command detection in noisy and cluttered environments. The TT-DNN component leverages the model parameter efficiency of a Transformer while maintaining the high performance characteristics of a Dense Neural Network. Our experiments indicate that, compared to conventional CNNs, the new framework achieves superior accuracy with significantly fewer parameters. Furthermore, when evaluated against state-of-the-art methods, the proposed system demonstrates superior robustness in identifying commands under adverse environmental conditions.

We investigate how to regulate the deterministic evolution of an open quantum system by employing a suitably chosen non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. This regulation is achieved through the application of time-dependent external driving forces to the system. We demonstrate that this approach enables the precise control of non-Hermitian dynamics, allowing for the creation of non-trivial trajectories, including those with complex-valued positions. Furthermore, we show that this framework permits the switching between different non-Hermitian evolutions, effectively treating the selection of a specific non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as a controllable process.

We introduce a plasmonic solar cell design utilizing a transparent conductive oxide substrate coated with a nanoparticle monolayer, followed by a thin active layer and a top electrode. This architecture enables the use of low-cost, thin-film materials for the active layer while leveraging the high absorption efficiency of plasmonic nanoparticles to capture light across the solar spectrum. We demonstrate that aluminum nanoparticles achieve a peak power conversion efficiency of 10.4% at a 100 nm active layer thickness, while gold nanoparticles yield an efficiency of 7.3% at 300 nm. This hybrid approach offers a viable pathway to enhance solar cell performance by utilizing inexpensive active layers alongside plasmonic nanoparticles as effective light-harvesting components.

Tensor decomposition methods are widely employed to optimize the performance of deep neural network (DNN) inference. Nevertheless, existing hardware accelerators predominantly prioritize throughput and energy efficiency, often neglecting the computational latency inherent in tensor decomposition. This oversight can result in latency bottlenecks that hinder the practical deployment of these accelerators in latency-sensitive applications. This paper introduces FDHT-LSTM, a model- and layer-aware, hardware accelerator designed specifically to mitigate latency issues in tensor decomposition. The system leverages a fully hard thresholding (FH) layer to execute hard threshold operations efficiently, alongside a fully hard proximal gradient (FHG) layer to accelerate tensor decomposition. The FDHT-LSTM architecture is specifically tailored for recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared to leading model-based hardware designs, the FDHT-LSTM achieves a 1.6x improvement in throughput, a 1.5x reduction in energy consumption, and a 1.5x reduction in latency.

UAVs are increasingly utilized in diverse sectors, including agriculture, security, and military operations. While MAVLink serves as a prevalent communication protocol for UAVs, it lacks inherent security, necessitating the implementation of encrypted channels. This study evaluates the efficiency of AES, RC4, and ChaCha20 algorithms for securing MAVLink messages. The findings indicate that RC4 offers the highest level of efficiency. Furthermore, the paper examines the computational requirements of the three algorithms and outlines the necessary hardware specifications for UAVs to support these cryptographic operations.

This paper introduces a method for constructing network emulators based on observed data. The core concept involves learning a reduced, abstract representation of a network by leveraging properties inherent in end-to-end measurements. This approach relies on the premise that, under specific conditions, these measurements reveal the network's structural topology. The technique is capable of modeling diverse network topologies, including those with complex interactions and multiple paths. Furthermore, the reduction process utilizes a data-driven strategy to identify and compactify nodes and links that exhibit similar behavior. Experimental results demonstrate that the networks reconstructed from this method closely match the original topology.

The Newman-Penrose formalism, which we present, offers a novel twistorial perspective on the map that connects a null geodesic congruence to a holomorphic curve within twistor space. Unlike the conventional approach, which maintains invariance solely under complex projective transformations of the twistor space itself, this formulation upholds invariance relative to the equivariant framework of both twistor space and sphere space.

The Muon Telescope Laboratory (MTL), situated at CERN, is a 10-meter deep underground muon detector designed to study cosmic ray muons. While primarily focused on fundamental physics, the MTL is also dedicated to investigating the potential of cosmic ray muon telescopes in archaeology. This paper details the deployment of the MTL for these archaeological studies, specifically highlighting its recent use in the first muon scan of the Egyptian sarcophagus known as Nefertari.

The Generalized LALR (GLL) method is a parsing technique that extends the capabilities of conventional LR parsing to support context-sensitive grammars. However, standard GLL algorithms suffer from ambiguity-induced redundancy, a flaw that has prompted numerous optimization efforts. This paper introduces PEGLL, a novel GLL algorithm grounded in the principle of pruning ambiguous parse trees. Unlike existing approaches, PEGLL retains support for grammar-macros while also incorporating a mechanism to detect and resolve conflicts arising from grammar rules. Experimental results indicate that PEGLL surpasses current state-of-the-art GLL implementations in terms of performance. Furthermore, because it accommodates grammar-syntax extensions, PEGLL offers superior versatility compared to other methods.

This study investigates the thermal radiation emitted by a charged black hole in a de Sitter space undergoing a Hawking transition to a hot, photon plasma background. By utilizing the worldline instanton formalism, we determine the tunneling rate of a charged particle escaping the black hole's event horizon. Our analysis reveals that the radiation rate initially rises with increasing temperature, attains a maximum value, and subsequently declines as the temperature continues to rise. Although the emission process remains kinematically feasible even in the high-temperature limit of an infinite photon bath, the radiation rate approaches zero in this specific limit. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the radiation rate exhibits a critical point at a finite temperature, signaling the occurrence of a first-order Hawking phase transition.

This study examines how linguistic context influences the neural representation of word predictability. Previous research indicates that the linguistic context surrounding a target word activates neural representations of that word, suggesting that measuring surprise based on the full linguistic context surrounding a target word better captures the surprise responses of comprehenders. To investigate this, we created a new dataset of word predictability scores that incorporates extended linguistic contexts. We then compared these long-context measures against the widely used van Gompel et al. (2006) short-context measures by evaluating their ability to forecast reading times during a sentence reading task. The findings indicate that long-context predictability measures are superior at forecasting reading times, especially for verbs and nouns, compared to the short-context measures. These results suggest that future research on language comprehension should employ long-context measures when assessing the predictive power of word frequency.

This paper introduces a new approach for 3D object pose estimation from single images, addressing the challenge of accurately learning canonical poses. We propose a multi-stage training scheme that progressively refines the estimation of canonical poses. This method is designed to overcome the limitations of prior work, which often fails to effectively capture fine-grained details in canonical poses due to the vast disparity in scale between this estimation task and the subsequent regression of camera poses. By mitigating this issue, the proposed approach enables the model to learn high-precision canonical poses, which in turn significantly enhances the accuracy of the estimated camera poses. Comprehensive experiments on the 3DObjectWNets and COICOD3D datasets confirm that this scheme substantially boosts performance.

We investigate the interplay between intrinsic spin-orbit coupling in indium antimonide (InSb) nanowires and external magnetic fields, specifically examining how this interaction influences the tunneling rates between quantum dots. Our analysis reveals that the resulting spin-orbit field induces a complex, non-monotonic dependence of the tunneling amplitude on the external magnetic field, a behavior that varies with the relative orientation of the two fields. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the specific magnetic field configuration can be utilized to manipulate the phase of the tunneling current, offering a novel pathway to control the current's characteristics in double quantum dot systems.

This study introduces a novel 2D simulation framework for radiation-dominated shocks, designed to incorporate pitch-angle scattering. This approach addresses the limitation of traditional 2D models, which fail to capture the scattering of particles out of the simulation plane. The model integrates the pitch-angle diffusion term into the Fokker-Planck equation, utilizing a Monte Carlo method to solve it. Simulations reveal that the newly developed 2D approach produces significantly harder particle spectra compared to standard 2D simulations. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the pitch-angle scattering rate is contingent upon the magnetic field geometry.

The precision measurement of the Higgs diphoton decay rate offers a robust constraint on the Higgsstrahlung process. This study examines the sensitivity of such constraints within an extended scalar sector featuring an additional charged Higgs boson. We demonstrate that combining this sensitivity with that of diboson production enables the exclusion of a Higgsstrahlung contribution that is 10% of the Standard Model prediction at the 95% confidence level, even when current experimental uncertainties are taken into account.

This article extends the definition of the common numerical radius for mappings to a broader setting. We examine how this extension relates to several fundamental properties, specifically addressing concepts such as joint numerical radius, the joint spectral radius, and the joint spectral radius of commuting operators. Additionally, the research connects these radius ideas to practical problems in best approximation and matrix scaling. A novel approach using the joint numerical radius for solving optimal scaling problems is introduced, with a specific focus on diagonal scaling.

Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) and the Privacy Amplification by Time Averaging of Enclaves (PATE) are two prominent approaches for applying privacy-preserving machine learning to financial data. This study evaluates their performance across various financial applications, comparing their utility-privacy trade-offs, computational efficiency, and implementation complexity. The findings indicate that DP-SGD consistently outperforms PATE in privacy metrics, while both methods demonstrate comparable ease of implementation.

This study extends the Wold-type decomposition framework by Davidson, Hertz, and Zinde-Walsh (2009) to accommodate broader classes of multivariate second-order stochastic processes. Specifically, we generalize this approach for the multivariate second-order random distribution fields defined by $X(\cdot)$, where $X(\cdot)$ is a stochastic process with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $h: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ belongs to a set of test functions. We demonstrate that the spectral density matrix $\mathbf{f}(\lambda)$ associated with such stochastic fields can be decomposed into three distinct components: a singular part, a deterministic component, and a singular part. This work establishes a novel link between the Wold-type decomposition and spectral analysis. Furthermore, we introduce a refined definition of the spectral density matrix for stochastic fields, which is grounded in the covariance operator of the stochastic field.

This study examines the impact of dust and impurities on the thermal explosion of a gas mixture under laser ignition. The analysis utilizes a two-dimensional model that accounts for the laser's influence on the ignition process, the formation of a soot layer, and the soot's absorption of thermal radiation. The research demonstrates that the proposed model effectively captures the impact of dust and impurities on the ignition characteristics of the mixture. The study also reveals that soot absorption of thermal radiation significantly influences the ignition process, with the impact becoming more pronounced as the concentration of dust increases.

This paper introduces a Boundary-Aware Segmentation Network (BANSN), designed to enhance the accuracy of semantic segmentation by incorporating boundary information. The proposed method utilizes a specialized module that integrates a boundary map with the primary segmentation input, enabling the network to capture both semantic and boundary details simultaneously. This module employs a multi-scale approach to handle boundaries of varying widths, ensuring robust feature extraction. The framework is validated on the Cityscapes dataset, where the model achieves a state-of-the-art mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 79.4%. Furthermore, we have developed two practical applications based on BANSN: a traffic sign detection system and a road delineation tool, both of which have been deployed in real-world scenarios.

This paper introduces the Driver's Message System (DMS), designed to warn drivers of safe opportunities to change lanes. The system utilizes a cooperative framework where vehicles exchange messages containing their current speed, intended speed, and the time required to reach the desired velocity. By analyzing these data points, the DMS identifies a target lane and calculates the optimal maneuvering time for the receiving vehicle. Through this mechanism, it informs drivers regarding when and where a lane change is safe. The proposed approach is evaluated using the SUMO traffic simulator, demonstrating its effectiveness in a controlled environment.

Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles (AOUPs) represent a prevalent model for studying out-of-equilibrium soft matter systems. This study examines the local density distribution of AOUPs in one and two dimensions under hard reflective boundaries, specifically analyzing conditions where the particle radius is commensurate with the boundary dimensions. The AOUP model incorporates Gaussian white noise for active forces alongside Ornstein-Uhlenbeck colored noise for inertia. By numerically solving the Fokker-Planck equation, we derive the steady-state probability density function and calculate local densities. The results demonstrate that non-uniform local density profiles emerge near the hard wall, with particle accumulation occurring when the radius equals the wall distance. The study further reveals that these profiles depend on both the particle's rotational inertia and the duration of its active force.

This study introduces a streamlined and efficient electronic structure methodology for ionized atoms and atoms within plasmas. The approach integrates Siegert time-dependent methods into the density functional theory framework tailored for average atom models. By applying this technique to hydrogenic systems, we demonstrate that incorporating the Siegert formalism yields substantial computational efficiency. Furthermore, we extend this approach to nonhydrogenic ionized atoms and plasma environments by employing a hybrid strategy that combines the random phase approximation with the random phase approximation with exchange.

This study examines the Si IV line profiles from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) during the July 2012 X1.4-class solar flare. We analyzed the Doppler shifts of both the primary and secondary peaks of the Si IV 10928 Å line profile. The redshifts observed in the secondary component align with the upward plasma flows reported by the Reuven Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic Explorer (RHESSO) and the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) during the flare's impulsive phase. Conversely, blueshifts detected in the primary component correspond to the downflows identified by both RHESSO and SDO/AIA. Furthermore, we investigated the temporal evolution of the secondary component's redshifts and found a correlation with the flare's X-ray light curve, suggesting that Si IV 10928 Å serves as a viable diagnostic tool for studying plasma dynamics within the solar corona.

We demonstrate that Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) offers a solution to the strong $CP$ problem even when $\alpha \neq 0$. This approach involves a scalar singlet field that spontaneously breaks $CP$ symmetry, thereby eliminating the need for fine-tuning. We provide a comprehensive overview of this mechanism and discuss its phenomenological consequences.

The study employs molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how ion bombardment influences the evolution of amorphous thin films. Utilizing geometric reasoning, the text demonstrates that the interface dynamic can be modeled by a specific equation, where the rate of change over time depends on the curvature of the boundary and the local energy density at that same boundary. Subsequent analysis reveals that the energy density at the interface is governed by an ordinary differential equation, with the energy loss rate being a function of the total energy within the system.

This article introduces the Router, a versatile data structure designed to store variable assignments. It demonstrates how integrating this Router into the source code enables effective plagiarism detection by hashing the executed path rather than the raw syntax, thereby securing software against simple copy-pasting and minor modifications. The article further details the implementation of the Router using a hash table and a trie, while also exploring the application of the Router within the context of detecting plagiarism in competitive programming.

This paper examines the class $\mathcal{Z}$ of Dirichlet series defined by the property $\lim_{x \to \infty} x^{\sigma_0} D(x) = \infty$, where $x \to \infty$ occurs along the abscissa of absolute convergence $\sigma_0$. We demonstrate that for any $\mathcal{Z}$-series, the abscissa of absolute convergence $\sigma_0$ satisfies the lower bound $\sigma_0 \geq 1/2$. This result extends a finding by A. M. Odlyzko, who established the same inequality specifically for $\mathcal{L}$-functions.

We demonstrate that imposing a bounded exponent on a group $G$ reduces its size to a finite collection of $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroups. Consequently, we derive that any finitely generated group $G$ satisfying the condition $p^n \equiv 1 \pmod m$ for all $n$ sufficiently large (where $p$ and $m$ are fixed integers) admits only finitely many irredicible cosets. This finding extends and refines earlier work by Breuillard, Guralnick, and Seress.

This study introduces novel algorithms for calculating log-concave maximum likelihood estimators (LME) with significantly improved computational efficiency. By integrating the recent framework of randomizing Nesterov smoothing with advanced algorithms designed for constrained optimization, these new methods achieve a complexity of $\tilde{O}(n)$ for computing the $\hat{p}$-th LME, where $0 < \hat{p} < n$. This represents a substantial improvement over the previous best-known complexity of $\tilde{O}(p \log p + p)$ for computing the $\hat{p}$-th LME, where $0 < \hat{p} \le n$. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that the new approach can be extended to handle the case of $\hat{p} > n$.

The non-interacting rigid arch (NIRA) model serves as a foundational framework for understanding the statistical mechanics of granular assemblies, offering insights into their stability and mechanical response. This study introduces a novel approach to derive the NIRA model directly from a standard contact model, specifically by applying a "stick-slip" rule to arches. This rule dictates that an arch remains stationary until a critical force threshold is breached, at which point it either splits or shifts. We demonstrate that this elementary rule captures essential characteristics of the full contact model, including the system's stability, the structural features of individual arches, and the collective dynamics of the ensemble. Furthermore, we illustrate that the NIRA model can be viewed as a specific limiting case of a broader class of contact models, where the transition between the two regimes is mediated by a tunable parameter.

We introduce a novel two-player game played on a graph, where optimal outcomes are determined by the maximum count of visitable vertices. In this framework, the two players take turns traversing an edge to an adjacent vertex; traversed edges are permanently removed from the graph. The game concludes when no valid moves remain, and the score equals the total number of visitable vertices. The primary objective is to determine the game value for a given graph, defined as the maximum or minimum outcome depending on which player starts. The paper presents a straightforward algorithm for bipartite graphs, which runs in linear time relative to the vertex and edge counts. For general graphs, the computational complexity is proven to be #P-hard.

The spectral density of stochastic processes is employed to differentiate between various types of random motion. We demonstrate that the spectral density of the fractional Langevin equation can be derived using the method of the Green function. Furthermore, the spectral properties of the fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process are analyzed through the application of the Riemann-Liouville fractional Brownian motion.

This study examines the initial value problem for the higher-order Broer-Kaup (HOBK) system, a general model describing dispersive water waves. The research confirms the global solvability of the HOBK system through a multi-step process. First, it establishes the well-posedness of an associated linear problem. Subsequently, the proof of global solvability for the HOBK system is achieved by applying fixed-point methods to these linear results. Finally, the paper derives blow-up criteria for strong solutions of the HOBK system, demonstrating the existence of finite-time singularities.

This paper investigates the existence of weak solutions to the two-dimensional nonhomogeneous Euler equations, where the fluid's viscosity is zero. The focus is on the scenario involving vorticity and a density gradient that are both aligned with a specific direction. We establish that energy conservation occurs when the vorticity and density gradients are co-planar, or when the vorticity oscillates rapidly in time and space relative to the density gradient.

This paper introduces VIRUP, a visualization software designed to support the development of interactive virtual representations of urban environments. Built upon the open-source VPython framework, VIRUP enables users to generate scripts for customizing viewports, including scene filtering, rendering sequences, and camera path creation. Developed as a Python-based library, the system provides user-friendly tools for constructing and managing 3D city models, as well as a web portal for data management and visualization. The authors detail VIRUP's architecture, its capabilities, and its implementation, while also presenting a case study involving a 3D urban representation of the city of Zurich.

The Data Bricks Space Mission offers a free, interactive, and engaging way to introduce data concepts to children aged 6 to 12. Participants can collect real-world data from NASA to uncover insights about the solar system, while also learning that data is vital for space exploration.

Data-paths in Software-Defined Networking (SDN) are typically defined through high-level specifications, yet verifying that the implemented paths align with these specifications remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a formal verification method for high-level SDN data-paths, utilizing the $\mu$CRL model checker to automatically check that $\mu$SDN models—extended $\mu$CRL models incorporating SDN concepts—satisfy their underlying high-level requirements. The discussion includes the development of a framework for modeling high-level SDN architectures, along with case studies demonstrating the method's application to the OpenFlow protocol.

Generative models are frequently evaluated based on their ability to disentangle latent representations, a metric that has become a standard for assessing the quality of generated outputs. However, this study demonstrates that an excessively strong disentanglement can hinder the model's capacity to perform controlled modifications to generated samples. Conversely, we propose "weak disentangling" as a viable alternative that maintains high-fidelity generation while enabling targeted manipulations. This approach relies on the concept that features which are semantically similar often reside in neighboring locations within the latent space. By intentionally grouping these related features into distinct clusters, we achieve effective control over the dimensions they represent. To implement this, we introduce a new objective function that encourages clustering among neighboring features while simultaneously enforcing a clustering constraint on the global latent distribution. Experimental results indicate that our method successfully balances the need for high-quality generation with the ability to perform specific edits, outperforming existing techniques in both metrics.

This study examines the aerodynamic performance of a two-dimensional tandem wing configuration, consisting of a leading and a trailing airfoil, through a series of numerical simulations. The investigation focuses on the influence of inter-airfoil vortex dynamics on overall efficiency. The analysis reveals that the strength of the leading edge vortices (LEVs) generated by the leading airfoil is highly sensitive to both the angle of attack and the relative position of the airfoils. These vortex structures significantly impact trailing airfoil performance by either enhancing lift or causing a loss in performance. The findings highlight that specific combinations of angle of attack and inter-airfoil spacing can synchronize the shedding of LEVs from both airfoils, resulting in a substantial boost to the trailing airfoil's performance.

Determining the real spectral function from Euclidean two-point data is a classic ill-posed challenge, which current methods attempt to solve by incorporating prior assumptions about the spectral function's form. This study introduces a new methodology that bypasses such manual priors by utilizing neural networks to perform a non-invertible mapping directly from Euclidean data to real-time physics. This approach is validated through a rigorous test using a massive scalar theory, where the real-time three-point function is reconstructed from Euclidean inputs. The reconstruction yields the three-particle threshold and the three-particle threshold velocity, demonstrating that the proposed technique successfully recovers real-time dynamics from Euclidean data without requiring predefined assumptions about the spectral function.

We demonstrate that a quantum dot can serve as a probe to determine the addition spectrum of a superconductor. By connecting the dot to the superconductor via two tunnel junctions, one can extract the energy required to add electrons to the superconductor. This method allows the detection of both the standard energy gap and, in certain cases, excited states within the gap. Our analysis shows that these measurements can be performed at temperatures significantly higher than the energy splitting between these intragap excited states.

The growing demand for pharmaceuticals has driven the development of computational methods to design drug molecules. While generative approaches have proven effective in creating molecules with desired properties, existing methods often fail to account for the constraints of real-world chemical synthesis. To address this, we introduce a new framework that integrates both chemical rules and property-based constraints into a unified generation process. By formulating chemical validity as executable rules, we enable the generation of valid molecules through logic-based filtering. Additionally, we introduce a specialized loss function that allows the model to learn the interplay between structural features and target properties. Our approach was evaluated on a dataset of 1,000 compounds, where the generated molecules successfully satisfied specific property targets while maintaining high synthetic feasibility.

This paper presents the Dynamic GoI Machine (DGoIM), a newly developed abstract machine designed to implement GoI's translation. We situate this machine within Accattoli's classification of abstract machines by confirming it functions as a dynamic machine, a status supported by the demonstration that it is a submachine of the GOOS machine.

This study introduces a machine learning approach for analyzing stellar populations in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) by leveraging the capabilities of the Gaia Data Release 2 (GDR2). We developed a model utilizing machine learning algorithms to classify LMC stars, achieving a precision of 99.9% and a recall rate of 98.7%. By applying this model to GDR2 data, we identified a sample of approximately 1.5 million LMC stars, which we further refined into a high-quality sample of roughly 1.2 million stars. We utilized the color-magnitude diagram (CMD) of this refined sample to examine the LMC's stellar populations, specifically targeting the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds' stellar streams. We also identified the LMC's thick and thin disks, as well as the LMC's halo. We also identified the LMC's thick and thin disks, as well as the LMC's halo.
